strengths: Significance: Deciding when further evaluations cease to justify their cost is a useful practical problem. The proposed EI(x) ≤ c(x) stopping condition is simple, interpretable, and accommodates spatially varying costs.

Originality: The equivalence between PBGI stopping and a zero threshold on LogEIPC provides a useful unifying interpretation. Extending the expected-cost argument to correlated Bayesian optimization adds understanding beyond the independent Pandora’s Box setting.

Empirical evidence: The evaluation crosses four acquisition functions with several stopping rules, covers synthetic objectives and six benchmark tasks, and reports results over 50 seeds with uncertainty bars. Figure 4 supports the practical competitiveness of the matched PBGI pair, and the appendix examines unknown costs and proxy-cost mismatch.

Presentation and ethics: The main methodological explanation is accessible, and the paper openly discusses model mismatch, acquisition optimization difficulties, and weaker results on two NATS datasets. LLM assistance is disclosed; no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: Lemma 1 is false as written. Its EI is conditioned on observations through t but evaluated at the already observed x_t, where noiseless EI is zero, so it cannot exceed positive c(x_t). The intended inequality should concern EI_{t−1}(x_t) for evaluations after initialization. Equation (15) repeats this conditioning error. Furthermore, the proof ends with a cumulative-cost bound, rather than explicitly establishing the stated cost-adjusted-regret bound. The intended telescoping argument appears repairable, but the central theorem requires corrected indexing, a completed proof, and conditions ensuring a well-defined terminal incumbent when the stopping time is potentially unbounded.

Theory–implementation gap: The guarantee relies on accepting only evaluations whose posterior expected improvement covers their cost. Section 3.2 introduces mandatory stabilization and debounce, while the 8D experiments use 20-iteration averaging. These modifications can permit evaluations that violate that inequality, so the theorem does not directly cover the evaluated procedure. Their sensitivity and effect on the guarantee are not established, and the abstract’s claim of freedom from heuristic tuning is too strong.

Experimental soundness: The claimed exact model-match experiments are inconsistent with Appendix C, which says kernel length scales are learned by maximum marginal likelihood in all experiments, whereas objectives are generated with length scale 0.1. A plug-in fitted posterior is not the exact generating posterior. Clarifying this distinction is necessary before interpreting these experiments as validation under the theorem’s assumptions.

Comparative significance: Most competing stopping thresholds remain fixed as the cost multiplier changes, although they target regret tolerances rather than the paper’s economic objective. These comparisons establish usefulness against literature defaults, but provide weaker evidence of superiority over appropriately calibrated alternatives. Cost-aware threshold sensitivity would strengthen the claim. Also, the hindsight comparator is optimal only along each acquisition policy’s realized trajectory, not globally over policies.

Reproducibility: Important implementation details are missing or contradictory. The stabilization and debounce lengths are unspecified; Appendix C gives a 200-iteration empirical cap, yet NATS plots extend to roughly 400 iterations. The stated PRB sample schedule uses max(ceil(64 × 1.5^{t−1}), 1000), contradicting the later description of at most 1000 samples and becoming infeasible at ordinary horizons. These discrepancies materially obstruct reproducing the results and runtime comparison.

Contribution scope: The main guarantee compares against stopping after initialization, rather than bounding suboptimality relative to an optimal correlated policy. Independent-case optimality follows from existing Pandora’s Box theory, and the stopping condition is a natural myopic improvement-versus-cost test. This remains a useful specialized contribution, but the unresolved theoretical and experimental issues currently outweigh its merits.

strengths: Significance: Deciding when further evaluations cease to justify their cost is a useful practical problem. The proposed EI(x) ≤ c(x) stopping condition is interpretable and accommodates spatially varying costs.

Originality: Section 3 provides a useful unifying interpretation of PBGI and LogEIPC stopping through the Pandora’s Box reservation value. Recomputing the stopping statistic after posterior updates is a reasonable extension to correlated objectives.

Evaluation: The experiments compare multiple acquisition–stopping combinations, use 50 seeds with uncertainty estimates, and cover synthetic objectives, six empirical tasks, several cost scales, and unknown or misspecified costs. The matched PBGI combination is competitive in many reported settings.

Presentation and limitations: The main methodological explanation is accessible. The authors acknowledge model mismatch, report unfavorable results on two NATS tasks, and disclose LLM assistance. I see no material research-ethics concern in the described work.
weaknesses: Soundness: Lemma 1 is false as indexed. It defines αEI_t using observations through t, then asserts αEI_t(x_t) ≥ c(x_t). In the noiseless setting, x_t is already observed and its expected improvement is zero. The intended statement concerns αEI_{t−1}(x_t) for 2 ≤ t ≤ τ; Equation (15) has the same conditioning error. Appendix B also finishes by bounding cumulative cost alone, rather than explicitly proving the stated cost-plus-regret bound. The intended result appears repairable by correctly indexing and telescoping expected improvements, but the central formal argument needs correction. Termination and the conditions justifying the stopping-time limit also need to be specified.

Theory–implementation gap: The abstract claims freedom from heuristic tuning, but Section 3.2 introduces a stabilization period and consecutive-trigger debounce, while the 8D experiments additionally average stopping statistics over 20 iterations. These modifications can permit evaluations whose expected improvement is below their cost, invalidating the proof’s key step. Their parameters and sensitivity are not adequately documented or ablated. Thus the guarantee does not establish the behavior of the practical procedure being evaluated.

Experimental validity: Section 4 describes the synthetic setting as having an exactly matched GP model, yet Appendix C says kernel length scales are learned by maximum marginal likelihood in all experiments, despite objectives being generated with fixed length scale 0.1. These are different inferential settings. A genuinely matched-prior experiment is needed to separate the theoretical stopping rule from hyperparameter estimation and stabilization effects.

Strength of evidence: Most competing stopping rules retain fixed accuracy tolerances while evaluation prices vary, so their poor cost-adjusted performance does not establish superiority over suitably calibrated alternatives. Sensitivity analyses or calibration on separate tasks would make this comparison more persuasive. The claimed empirical advantage of stopping after posterior updates is supported in Figure 10 by only one sampled function, rather than a repeated ablation.

Originality and theoretical significance: The rule closely extends established EI-versus-cost stopping and Weitzman stopping; the equivalence follows directly from monotonicity of EI. Theorem 2 provides a useful but limited no-worse-than-immediate guarantee, shared by any policy selecting only evaluations with nonnegative expected net improvement, as Appendix B itself acknowledges. It supplies no approximation guarantee relative to optimal correlated search. Corollary 3 additionally requires U, whose practical estimation is not demonstrated; choosing U = 50 from an objective range of [0,100] does not by itself establish a valid bound.

Reproducibility and reporting: Several details conflict or remain unclear. Appendix C specifies PRB sample counts using max(ceil(64 × 1.5^(t−1)), 1000), whereas Appendix D describes at most 1000 samples. Empirical experiments reportedly stop at a 200-iteration cap, but Figures 15–17 extend to 400. The one-evaluation Immediate baseline also needs reconciliation with initialization using 2(d+1) samples, including how initialization costs are counted. Table 1’s assertion of identical failure counts across acquisition functions needs clarification. Together with unspecified stabilization/debounce settings and no code-availability statement, these issues prevent reliable reconstruction of the reported comparisons.

strengths: Significance: Cost-aware stopping addresses a practical gap in Bayesian optimization. Optimizing simple regret plus evaluation cost makes the stopping decision economically interpretable and exposes overspending that accuracy-only evaluations can obscure.

Originality: The equivalence between the PBGI stopping condition and stopping when every point has expected improvement at most its cost (Equations 8–10) provides a useful unification of two acquisition functions. Updating the stopping decision using the latest posterior is natural.

Empirical evidence: The evaluation covers multiple acquisition–stopping combinations, three synthetic cost functions, six empirical tasks, and 50 seeds with uncertainty bars. Figure 4 supports the competitiveness of the matched PBGI combination, while the additional runtime-proxy and unknown-cost experiments broaden the evidence.

Presentation and limitations: The main intuition is accessible, and the manuscript acknowledges model mismatch, acquisition-optimization errors, and weaker performance on two NATS tasks. The noiseless scope and possible extensions are stated. I identified no material research-ethics concern; LLM assistance is disclosed.
weaknesses: Soundness: Lemma 1 is false as indexed. It defines expected improvement conditional on observations through t, then claims that this quantity at the already observed x_t exceeds its positive cost. In the noiseless setting that expected improvement is zero. The intended statement is about x_{t+1} given observations through t, or x_t given observations through t−1, and excludes the unconditional first evaluation. Equation 15 repeats this conditioning error. The underlying argument appears repairable, but the central formal statements require correction.

Theorem 2's proof ends by establishing a cumulative-cost bound in Equation 19, rather than explicitly establishing the stated cost-adjusted-regret bound. The latter can plausibly be recovered from the telescoping identity after correcting the indexing, but the proof should complete that step and justify the stopping-time argument. Compactness and pointwise positive costs alone also do not establish finite termination. Furthermore, the text claims 'strictly better' performance although the theorem only guarantees non-inferiority.

The implemented method differs materially from the guaranteed policy. Section 3.2 adds mandatory stabilization and consecutive-trigger debouncing; the 8D experiments additionally use a 20-iteration moving average. These mechanisms can continue evaluations after expected improvement falls below cost, invalidating the per-step premise of the guarantee. Their contribution is not isolated through ablations, and the abstract's claim of being free of heuristic tuning is therefore too strong. Learning GP hyperparameters in Appendix C also complicates the claim that the synthetic experiments exactly match the assumed Bayesian model.

The evidence for comparative superiority needs stronger calibration. Most competing thresholds remain fixed while evaluation costs vary, although those methods primarily target accuracy rather than the paper's economic objective. Cost-dependent threshold sweeps would distinguish advantages of the proposed rule from advantages of matching its threshold to the evaluation metric. Also, Hindsight optimizes stopping along each acquisition policy's own trajectory; proximity to it does not establish proximity to the optimal acquisition-and-stopping policy.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the useful setup appendix. The manuscript does not provide a code link, exact stabilization/debounce settings, or sufficient details of continuous GP sampling and acquisition optimization in 8D. The PRB sample schedule is written as max(ceil(64 × 1.5^(t−1)), 1000), whereas Appendix D describes up to 1000 samples; this consequential inconsistency needs resolution. It should also specify how costs are transformed when empirical objective values are standardized.

The theoretical contribution is useful but limited: independent-case optimality comes from classical Pandora's Box theory, and the correlated-case guarantee compares against stopping immediately, without an approximation guarantee to an optimal policy. The budget application additionally requires a justified value or upper bound for U. Appendix D's choice U = 50 does not follow from the [0,100] range alone, and halving the cost multiplier in PBGI-D does not preserve the fixed-multiplier budget guarantee. These issues, together with the gap between the analyzed and evaluated policies, warrant revision before acceptance.

strengths: Significance: Cost-aware stopping addresses a useful practical problem that fixed budgets and regret-only stopping criteria do not directly solve. Comparing acquisition-function–stopping-rule pairs is particularly valuable.

Soundness: The equivalence between PBGI stopping and requiring expected improvement to exceed evaluation cost is convincing. Under correct posterior inference and exact acquisition optimization, the telescoping argument supporting Theorem 2 is sound and yields useful expected-cost and termination bounds.

Originality: The contribution is primarily a unifying interpretation of existing acquisition and stopping principles. Connecting PBGI and LogEIPC through a shared stopping criterion, and extending the analysis to correlated objectives, provides useful understanding.

Evaluation: The experiments cover multiple cost scales, synthetic problems, 35 LCBench datasets, and three NATS-Bench datasets, with 50 seeds and uncertainty estimates. Per-dataset results, hindsight references, and additional actual-runtime and unknown-cost experiments strengthen the evidence.

Presentation and limitations: The core derivation is clear, and the paper openly reports underperforming datasets and discusses model mismatch. The noiseless scope is explicit, LLM assistance is disclosed, and no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: The practical algorithm differs materially from the analyzed rule. Section 3.2 introduces a stabilization period and consecutive-trigger debouncing, while Section 4.1 and Appendix C describe 20-iteration moving averages. These modifications can continue sampling when expected improvement is below cost, invalidating the key premise of Lemma 1. Their precise relationship, parameter choices, and effects are insufficiently established. An ablation separating the exact rule from these modifications is needed, particularly given the claim of avoiding heuristic tuning.

The claimed model-matched synthetic evaluation is inconsistent with the implementation description. Section 4 says the GP exactly matches the generating process, whose length scale is 0.1, but Appendix C says length scales are learned by maximum marginal likelihood in all experiments. Plug-in hyperparameter estimation does not provide the exact generating posterior. This needs clarification or a genuinely matched experiment before the synthetic results can support the stated interpretation.

The theoretical advance is limited in strength: Theorem 2 guarantees only performance no worse than immediate stopping, not proximity to an optimal stopping policy or a useful terminal-regret target. The argument applies to any policy whose conditional expected improvement covers its cost, as the appendix acknowledges. Corollary 4 also requires an available value or valid bound for U; the experimental choice U = 50 is not justified merely by classification error lying in [0,100].

Reproducibility requires revision. No code repository is identified, and important details remain unclear, including continuous GP sample generation and optimum estimation in 8D, stabilization/debounce settings, and how cost units are handled alongside output standardization. There are also concrete reporting conflicts: Appendix D.3 says unknown-cost experiments use LogEIPC-exp, whereas Figure 18 labels LogEIPC-inv; Appendix C specifies a 200-iteration empirical cap, whereas Figures 14–16 extend beyond it.

The empirical comparisons do not fully establish the claimed robustness. Baseline stopping thresholds are largely fixed across cost scales, so sensitivity analyses would help distinguish benefits of cost calibration from benefits of the proposed rule. Actual-runtime and unknown-cost tests cover only three LCBench datasets. Furthermore, evaluation uses test error while acquisition and stopping use validation error, so empirical violations of the theoretical behavior cannot be attributed solely to GP misspecification. These issues, together with the implementation discrepancies, warrant revision before the contribution can be reliably reproduced.

strengths: Soundness: The equivalence between the PBGI stopping condition and EI(x) ≤ c(x) is convincing. Theorem 2 has a sound core argument: conditional expected improvements cover evaluation costs, and realized improvements telescope. This provides a useful Bayesian guarantee under exact posterior inference and acquisition optimization.

Significance: Deciding when further optimization is worth its cost is a practical problem. The proposed rule is simple, interpretable, and readily integrates with existing PBGI and LogEIPC implementations.

Evaluation: The experiments cover multiple cost scales and cost functions, 1D and 8D synthetic problems, 35 LCBench datasets, and three NATS-Bench tasks, with 50 seeds and uncertainty bars. Comparisons against immediate and hindsight stopping help contextualize performance. Figures 2–3 provide credible evidence of usefulness, particularly with PBGI.

Presentation and limitations: The manuscript clearly develops the decision problem and its connection to Pandora’s Box. It reports unfavorable datasets and includes unknown-cost and cost-mismatch experiments rather than concealing failures. The noiseless scope and possible extensions are acknowledged. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Originality and theoretical significance are limited. The rule combines an existing Pandora’s Box stopping condition with the familiar principle of stopping when expected improvement no longer covers cost. Theorem 2 guarantees only performance no worse than immediate stopping; it gives no approximation guarantee relative to an optimal correlated policy. Appendix B correctly observes that the same argument applies to any policy satisfying the one-step improvement condition.

The analyzed and implemented procedures differ materially. Section 3.2 introduces stabilization and debounce safeguards, while Appendix C uses 20-iteration averaging in 8D. These can permit evaluations whose expected improvement is below cost, so Lemma 1 does not automatically cover the implemented algorithm. Sensitivity studies and ablations are needed to establish how much performance depends on these safeguards and to qualify the claim of avoiding heuristic tuning.

The supposedly model-matched synthetic evaluation is not fully specified consistently: Section 4 describes exact model matching, but Appendix C says kernel length scales are learned by marginal likelihood in all experiments, whereas generating functions use length scale 0.1. Sharing a kernel family does not ensure the posterior is the true conditional distribution required by the proof.

Baseline comparisons establish performance against particular default settings, rather than well-calibrated alternatives for the same economic objective. Most comparator thresholds remain fixed while cost scales vary. Cost-dependent threshold sweeps or held-out calibration would strengthen the claim that the proposed rule improves on existing stopping approaches.

Reproducibility has concrete gaps. The stabilization duration and precise debounce implementation are not specified; the single-point initialization in the theorem and Immediate description needs reconciliation with the experimental initialization of 2(d+1) samples. Appendix C specifies PRB sample counts using max(ceil(64·1.5^(t−1)), 1000), which conflicts with Appendix D’s description of up to 1000 samples. No code availability statement is provided.

Some empirical interpretations overreach. Hindsight stopping is optimal only along each acquisition policy’s sampled trajectory, not across all adaptive policies. The attribution of poor performance to model misspecification is plausible but unverified, especially because empirical acquisition optimizes validation error while reported regret uses test error. These distinctions should temper claims of near-optimality and robustness.

strengths: Soundness: The equivalence between the PBGI stopping condition and EI(x) ≤ c(x) is convincing. Lemma 1 and the telescoping argument in Theorem 2 establish a useful guarantee under exact posterior inference and acquisition optimization: expected cost-adjusted regret does not exceed immediate stopping. The cumulative-cost and termination consequences follow naturally.

Significance: Deciding when further evaluations cease to justify their cost is practically important. The proposed rule is simple, accommodates spatially varying costs, and integrates directly with two established acquisition functions.

Originality: The contribution is primarily a useful unification and analysis of existing decision principles. Connecting Pandora’s Box stopping to cost-aware EI, and deriving a guarantee for correlated objectives, provides meaningful understanding even though the underlying one-step stopping principle is familiar.

Evaluation: The experiments cover several cost functions and scales, synthetic problems, 35 LCBench datasets, and three NATS-Bench datasets, with 50 seeds and uncertainty estimates. Comparing acquisition–stopping combinations and including trajectory-specific hindsight references helps distinguish acquisition quality from stopping quality. Figures 2–3 support competitive performance, particularly with PBGI.

Presentation and research practice: The main derivation is clear, and the appendices provide substantial experimental detail. The authors explicitly report unsuccessful cases, discuss model mismatch, and disclose LLM assistance. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantee is limited: it compares against immediate stopping, rather than an optimal adaptive policy, and provides no approximation ratio or quantitative characterization of premature stopping. Appendix B correctly notes that the same argument applies to any policy whose expected one-step improvement covers its cost. This limits the theorem’s distinctiveness and the strength of the resulting optimality interpretation.

The practical implementation falls outside the proved guarantee. Stabilization periods, debounce logic, and 20-iteration averaging can permit evaluations after their expected improvement falls below cost. Consequently, the abstract’s claim of operating 'without heuristic tuning' is too strong. Ablations of these safeguards and a clearer separation between the analyzed and implemented policies would strengthen the paper.

Baseline comparisons do not fully isolate the benefit of the stopping principle. Most competing rules use fixed literature thresholds targeting regret or convergence rather than the evaluated cost-adjusted objective. Limited threshold sensitivity or calibration using separate tasks would make superiority claims more convincing. Moreover, Figure 9 supports the claimed advantage of checking after posterior updates with only one illustrative function draw.

Reproducibility contains consequential ambiguities. Section 4 describes exact GP model match, whereas Appendix C says kernel length scales are learned in all experiments. Figure 18 labels the acquisition LogEIPC-inv, while its caption and Appendix D.3 describe LogEIPC-exp; this distinction matters to the claimed guarantee. The paper should also specify how costs are rescaled when objective outputs are standardized, and provide the numerical acquisition-optimization settings and implementation.

The limitations are honestly reported, but their explanations remain tentative. Small dataset size alone does not establish GP misspecification as the cause of failures. Furthermore, the empirical policy optimizes validation error while reported regret uses test error, introducing another source of discrepancy from the theoretical objective. Unknown-cost results cover only three LCBench tasks, so evidence for that extension is substantially narrower than the main benchmark coverage.
